transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. Before we begin, could you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's—it's a bit hard to explain, but I'll try my best to give you the full picture, because I think context is really important here. You see, I’ve always been someone who thrives on structure and staying engaged. For years, I’ve worked as an executive administrative assistant, so keeping a clean, meticulously organized calendar is practically in my blood. And outside of work, I have my routines, things that really make me feel like *me*. I go on these photography walks—every Sunday morning, usually around the botanical gardens or down by the river, trying to catch the early light, you know? And I also mentor some kids at the community center on Tuesday evenings. I’ve done that for over a decade. But lately... well, that’s what made me come in. All of those things, the things that usually give my week shape and make me feel alive, they just started feeling so... flat. And heavy. It’s not even that I’m actively sad about them, it’s more like the spark just fizzled out completely. I’d look at my camera sitting by the door and just think, "Why bother?" I’d look at my calendar, which usually gives me a sense of satisfaction to organize, and it just looked like a wall of meaningless blocks. I just stopped initiating any of it. I haven't picked up the camera in weeks, I've been calling out of the mentoring sessions, and I just sit there feeling this strange, empty weight. It’s like the engine just shut off, and I don't know how to turn the key again. I just can't seem to muster the drive to do the things I know I should be doing, the things I usually love doing.
How long have you been feeling this way—when did you first notice this shift in your mood and motivation?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back—and I have thought about this a lot, because I'm the type of person who likes to find the root cause of things, you know, track the timeline—it’s, um, it’s been about a year and three months now. Yes, a year and three months. 

I know that specifically because it all started right after a situation with a family member of mine. Their health took a pretty drastic turn, and along with that, their behavior changed entirely. They became very unpredictable, very difficult to navigate, and it was just this massive upheaval for our whole family. And naturally—because of what I do for a living, because I’m the one who knows how to manage schedules and handle logistics and keep a cool head—the bulk of the responsibility fell squarely on my shoulders. 

I had to step in and take on all this extra coordination. I was making the phone calls, setting up the appointments, trying to manage their daily life on top of my own, just constantly putting out fires and trying to keep everything from completely falling apart. It was like I was suddenly working a second full-time job as a crisis manager. And it was just so much. 

It was right around that time, when I was pouring all my organizational energy into their situation, that I noticed my own life starting to slip. I’d come home from dealing with all their chaos, and that’s when that heavy, flat feeling I was telling you about really set in. I thought it was just temporary burnout, you know? Just a phase because of all the extra coordination and stress I was under. But here we are, fifteen months later, and even on the days when things with them are quiet, I still can’t seem to get my own spark back. So, yes, about a year and a quarter of feeling exactly like this, just completely stalled out.
Before this past year and three months, had you ever gone through a similar period of low mood, low energy, and loss of interest that lasted for weeks or more, at any earlier point in your life?

No, actually. And that's another thing I've spent a lot of time reflecting on, trying to comb through my past to see if there was a precedent for this, because I like to look for patterns. In my line of work, if there's a problem, you look at the historical data, right? You see if this issue has cropped up in previous quarters. So I really dug deep into my own history. 

I thought back to my twenties, when I first started out in the administrative field, which was incredibly stressful, and then my thirties, when I moved to this city and had to completely rebuild my social circle and find new routines. There were stressful times, certainly. Times I was tired or overwhelmed by a big project or a demanding boss. But never this. Never this complete... evaporation of my drive. 

I was always the person who bounced back. If I had a tough week, I'd just make sure my Sunday morning photo walk was extra long, or I'd throw myself into planning a really engaging activity for the kids at the center, and that would recharge my batteries. I never had a period where I just stopped caring or stopped functioning in my personal life for weeks on end. This feeling, this absolute flatness where I can't even bring myself to care about my own hobbies, it's completely unprecedented for me. It's like I'm dealing with a totally new variable that I have no previous data for, which is incredibly frustrating for someone who prides himself on being prepared and knowing how to manage things. So, no, nothing like this before the situation with my family member started.

Over these past several months, has this low mood and lack of drive affected your ability to keep up with your work responsibilities or your day-to-day self-care, like eating, sleeping, or personal hygiene?

Well, it’s a really interesting question, and one I’ve actually been trying to quantify myself, because, as you can probably tell by now, I’m someone who measures my success by my output and my reliability. So, if we look at work first—I haven't lost my job or anything drastic like that. Overall, the structure of my work has stayed intact. I still show up, I still sit at my desk, I still answer the phones. But... the quality of my work, the precision that I’m known for? That’s definitely taken a hit. 

You see, usually, managing a complex calendar for three different executives is like second nature to me. I can see the conflicts before they happen, I know exactly how much travel time to buffer between meetings, I know who prefers a morning slot versus an afternoon slot. But lately, over these past several months, I’ve been missing details. I’ll forget to send the Zoom link, or I’ll accidentally double-book a conference room. And these are things that used to be completely automatic for me. Now, I find myself having to double-check, sometimes triple-check, every single task, every email I send, because I just don't trust my own brain right now. It takes me twice as long to do half the work, and the mental energy required just to maintain that facade of competence is exhausting. 

And then, as for my day-to-day life and the things outside of work... well, like I mentioned before, I’ve really pulled back. The photography outings? I just don't go. I used to pack a lunch, make a whole day of it, really immerse myself in the environment. Now, the thought of even charging the battery on my camera feels like an insurmountable chore. And the mentoring at the community center... that's been the hardest part to admit, honestly. I've been calling out, telling them I'm sick or that I have a scheduling conflict, which I hate doing because I pride myself on being dependable. But I just don't feel present. I don't feel like I have anything of value to offer those kids right now. I’m not reliable. If I can't even keep my own calendar straight at work, how can I be a steady presence for them? 

As for the self-care stuff—eating, sleeping, hygiene—I’m still showering, I’m still putting on a suit every day, because I have to. The routine of getting dressed for work is so ingrained in me that I just go through the motions. But eating? I’ve definitely been slipping there. I used to meal prep every Sunday—very organized, perfectly portioned containers for the whole week. Now, I just grab whatever is easiest, or I forget to eat lunch entirely because I’m so bogged down trying to double-check my work. So, yes, while the scaffolding of my life is still standing, the actual day-to-day functioning is... it’s definitely compromised. It’s like I’m operating at a fifty percent capacity, at best, and it takes one hundred percent of my effort just to maintain that.
Have you had any thoughts about death, dying, or that you'd be better off not being here, or any thoughts of harming yourself?

Well, no, actually. I know that's a standard question, and I completely understand why you have to ask it, especially given everything I've just laid out about how drastically my productivity and my general engagement with life have dropped. It makes total sense that you'd need to check that box. But no, I haven't had any thoughts about dying or harming myself, or feeling like people would be better off without me. 

Even with this heavy, flat feeling, and the intense frustration of operating at a fraction of my usual capacity, my brain just doesn't really go to that kind of dark place. I think a lot of it comes back to how I process the world. I'm a fixer, you know? I'm a planner. If I were to, um, just not be here, the sheer logistical nightmare that would leave behind—for my office, for the three executives I support, and especially for my family, who, as I mentioned, are already dealing with that massive ongoing upheaval with my relative—it's just completely unthinkable to me. 

I mean, if I’m not there, who sorts out the quarterly scheduling conflicts? Who manages the care coordination for my family? I've spent my entire adult life, my whole career, building these systems and making sure the people around me are supported and everything runs like clockwork. So even when I feel completely stalled out, even on the days when I'm staring at my camera battery and I just can't bring myself to plug it into the wall, I'm still fundamentally tethered to my responsibilities. I might feel empty, and I might be exhausted from double-checking my emails all day, but I certainly don't want to die. I just want to figure out how to get my efficiency back, you know? I want to solve the problem, not escape it. So, no, absolutely no thoughts of self-harm or anything along those lines. It's just... it's just not in my nature to leave a project unfinished.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a single, first-lifetime episode (no prior history) of persistently depressed/flat mood and pervasive anhedonia (loss of interest in photography and mentoring) lasting over a year, well beyond the 2-week threshold. Associated symptoms include anergia, impaired concentration/attention (errors at work, need for repeated double-checking), appetite disturbance, and significant functional impairment at work and in personal life, though the patient maintains basic self-care and job attendance. No psychotic features, no history of manic/hypomanic episodes, and no suicidal ideation. The symptom cluster and moderate functional impairment (reduced efficiency but not complete incapacity) meet criteria for a Moderate Depressive Episode (F32.1) rather than mild (F32.0) or severe (F32.2) depression. Onset followed a significant psychosocial stressor (family caregiving crisis), but the reaction has evolved into a full depressive syndrome exceeding an adjustment disorder (F43.21) in duration, severity, and symptom breadth, making major depressive episode the better fit.
